Probabilistic data structures in Go, part 2

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3254 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Antonz

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, probabilistic data structures give you approximate answers to questions about the data they handle.
  • Previously, we reviewed the following data structures: Bloom filter (for checking if an item is in a set), Count-min sketch (for counting items), HyperLogLog (for counting unique items), T-digest (for finding quantiles), and Top-k (for finding the most frequent items).
  • In this post, we'll talk about other probabilistic structures and compare them to the ones we've already covered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, probabilistic data structures give you approximate answers to questions about the data they handle. Does the set contain a certain item? How many unique items are in the collection? What is the 99th percentile in a stream of numbers? How similar are two sets? Unlike deterministic structures, the answers might not be exact, but in return, you can save a lot of memory.

Previously, we reviewed the following data structures: Bloom filter (for checking if an item is in a set), Count-min sketch (for counting items), HyperLogLog (for counting unique items), T-digest (for finding quantiles), and Top-k (for finding the most frequent items).

In this post, we'll talk about other probabilistic structures and compare them to the ones we've already covered. We'll look at how they work and what kinds of guarantees they provide.

All examples use unsure — a package that implements these structures in Go.

Binary fuse filter • UltraLogLog • Log-linear histogram • MinHash.

A binary fuse filter is a set that trades certainty for space, like a Bloom filter1. It can tell you that an item is definitely not in the set, or that it probably is (which might be a false positive). The filter doesn't store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular set.

According to recent reports, unlike a Bloom filter, a binary fuse filter is static: you build it once from all the items, and you can't add more later. In exchange, it uses less memory than a Bloom filter with the same false positive rate. For example, a fuse filter for 1,000,000 items with a 0.39% false positive rate takes 1.13 MB (9 bits per item), while a Bloom filter takes 1.51 MB (12 bits per item).

This makes binary fuse filters a good fit for data that is written once and read many times, like the key set of an immutable file in a database (to skip files that don't have the key), or a list of known bad items, such as leaked passwords or malicious URLs.

The fingerprint type (T in Upcoming[T]) determines the false positive rate and the memory use:.

In a recent development, the constructor takes an iterator of items to add to the filter and the expected number of items (0 if unknown). The number is only used to preallocate memory, so a good estimate makes the build faster.

You can check if an item is in the filter, but you cannot add or delete an item, count the number of items, or iterate over them.

The filter2 is an array of b-bit fingerprints (for example, b = 8 for uint8). Each item is hashed to a 64-bit value h, which gives the item's fingerprint f (b bits computed from h) and three positions in the array (cells). The array is filled so that for every item, the XOR of its cells equals f.

To check an item, you compute h, look up its three cells, and compare their XOR with f. For an item in the set, they always match. For any other item, the XOR is a random b-bit value, which matches f with probability 2^-b.

Each check reads three cells, so for large filters it's three cache misses, against one for a blocked Bloom filter. However, since the reads are independent, the CPU can do them concurrently, so the checks are about as fast as with a Bloom filter.

Sources indicate that the filter uses the local wyhash3 implementation for hashing. It performs roughly the same as xxh34 but has a much simpler implementation, without SIMD or assembly.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks5, comparing unsure to xorfilter6 (binary fuse by the authors of the paper) and bloom (unsure's own Bloom filter) with 8-bit fingerprints (ns/op, lower is better):.

Memory, bits per item (lower is better):.

Unsure is the same size as xorfilter (same layout) with up to 25% faster checks. Compared to the Bloom filter, it uses up to 36% less memory, with checks as fast or faster, but up to 2.5× slower builds.

Recent findings suggest that bloom filter overview and how it works. ↩︎.

Industry observers note that binary Fuse Filters paper by Thomas Mueller Graf and Daniel Lemire, 2022. ↩︎.

Industry observers note that reference wyhash implementation by Wang Yi. ↩︎.

Reference xxHash implementation by Yann Collet. ↩︎.

Sources indicate that binary fuse filter benchmarks. ↩︎.

FastFilter/xorfilter by Daniel Lemire. ↩︎.

Recent findings suggest that ultraLogLog is a unique items counter that trades accuracy for space, like HyperLogLog7. It tells you approximately how many distinct items it has seen, no matter how many times each one appeared. UltraLogLog doesn't store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular set.

UltraLogLog is a newer design (Otmar Ertl, 2024) that uses the space more efficiently: for the same error, it needs about 43% less memory than HyperLogLog. For example, a HyperLogLog sketch with 0.81% standard error takes 16 KB, while an UltraLogLog sketch with 0.86% error takes 8 KB. However, adding, counting, and merging are slower than with HyperLogLog.

UltraLogLog is useful in the same places as HyperLogLog: counting unique visitors, unique search queries, or distinct values in a database column, possibly across many machines or segments.

You can merge sketches to get the total number of unique items from all of them, without counting shared items twice.

Sources indicate that the sketch has one setting: the precision p, which gives a relative standard error of 0.782/√(2^p). The default is p=13 with 0.86% error in 8 KB, close to the common HyperLogLog default (0.81% in 16 KB).

You can add items to a sketch, get the estimated count, and merge sketches. You cannot check if a specific item was added, remove items, or list them.

It has been revealed that hyperLogLog hashes each item and uses the first p bits of the hash to pick one of m = 2^p registers. It calculates the rank (the number of leading zeros in the rest of the hash, plus one) and keeps the highest rank it has seen in the register. Seeing a rank of k suggests there were about 2^k items in the register. The count is estimated from all the registers together.

Sources indicate that A HyperLogLog register loses some information: it only keeps track of the highest value, not whether any slightly lower values were seen. These lower values show up at least as often as the highest one, so they can tell a lot about the count.

In a recent development, ultraLogLog8 uses the registers more efficiently. Each register is still one byte, but it stores the highest rank k in the upper 6 bits, and whether k−1 and k−2 were seen in the lower 2 bits:.

The count estimate uses the FGRA estimator from the UltraLogLog paper. Each register adds a weight based on its value, and the count is calculated as a power of the sum of the weights. Nearly empty and nearly full sketches get special handling, so the estimate stays accurate from zero to billions of items, without bias tables or a separate formula for small counts.

In a recent development, unsure keeps a histogram of register values (256 four-byte counters, 1 KB) updated as the registers change. This way, Count reads the histogram instead of scanning all the registers. Merge checks 8 registers at a time using a few bitwise operations to find which ones the other sketch would change, and only updates those.

The item is hashed once with wyhash, and the 64-bit hash is split into the register index and the rank.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks9, comparing UltraLogLog to unsure's own HyperLogLog and axiom10 (HyperLogLog with LogLog-Beta estimator and sparse mode) (ns/op, lower is better):.

Accuracy and memory, relative RMSE over 1,000 sketches (lower is better):.

UltraLogLog provides the same accuracy as HyperLogLog with almost half the memory. However, adding, counting, and merging are noticeably slower.

In a recent development, hyperLogLog overview and how it works. ↩︎.

Industry observers note that ultraLogLog paper by Otmar Ertl, 2024. ↩︎.

axiomhq/hyperloglog by Axiom. ↩︎.

A log-linear histogram is a summary of a stream of numbers that trades accuracy for space. It can give you an approximate median, 99th percentile, or any other quantile of the data. It can also estimate what fraction of the numbers are below a certain value (the CDF). The histogram doesn't store the numbers, so it's much more compact than a sorted list.

It has been revealed that for example, to find the exact 99th percentile of 1,000,000 response times, you'd have to keep all of them. With 64-bit floats, that takes 8 MB. A log-linear histogram estimates the same percentile within 0.39% of its true value using about 14 KB — almost 600 times less.

Industry observers note that the error is relative to the value: if the true 99th percentile is 200 ms, the histogram returns a value between 199.2 and 200.8 ms. This guarantee applies to every quantile, from the median to the most extreme outliers. The size of the histogram doesn't depend on the number of values, only on the accuracy you choose and on how wide the range of the values is.

A log-linear histogram is useful when you need percentiles for positive values that cover a wide range, like latencies, file sizes, or prices.

You can merge histograms to gather data from multiple machines or segments (like by hour, endpoint, or region). Merging is exact: a merged histogram is the same as if it had received all the values directly.

Industry observers note that the histogram has two settings: relative error and value range. By default, the error is 0.0039 (0.39%) and the range is from 1e-9 to 1e18. Lowering the error or increasing the range uses more memory.

You can add numbers to a histogram, estimate quantiles and the CDF, and merge histograms. You cannot remove numbers or list them.

According to recent reports, A histogram splits the range of values into buckets and counts how many values are in each one. To estimate a quantile, it adds up the counts starting from the lowest bucket until it reaches the requested rank, then returns a value from that bucket. The accuracy of the estimate depends on how wide the bucket is.

With buckets that have equal widths, like 0–10, 10–20, and so on, every estimate has the same absolute error of ±5 around the bucket's midpoint. So the relative error is very large for small values and unnecessarily small for large values:.

In a recent development, A logarithmic histogram solves this by making each bucket's width proportional to its value. For example, if the bucket boundaries are powers of 1.02 (1, 1.02, 1.0404, ...), the end of each bucket is 2% larger than its start, so any value in the bucket is within about 1% of the bucket's midpoint. DDSketch11 uses this method. The downside is that finding the right bucket for a value means you have to calculate a logarithm, which is relatively slow.

Recent findings suggest that A log-linear histogram gets almost the same result with cheaper math. First, it splits the values into ranges between powers of two: 1–2, 2–4, 4–8, and so on (these are called octaves). Then it splits every octave into the same number of equal-width buckets. For example, here are three octaves with 4 buckets each:.

Each octave is twice as long as the previous one, so its buckets are twice as wide, and the bucket width grows with the values, as in a logarithmic histogram. Finding the right bucket only takes a few bit operations instead of calculating a logarithm.

In a recent development, hdrHistogram12 is the best-known log-linear histogram. It records integers: the position of the highest 1 bit of a number determines its octave, and the next few bits determine the bucket within the octave.

Unsure works with float64 numbers and finds the bucket in a similar way to HdrHistogram.

IEEE 754 double-precision format.

A float64 in Go (and most other languages) is made up of three parts:.

The number's value is 1.f × 2^e, where 1.f is a binary fraction between 1 and 2.

The exponent determines the octave, from 2^e to 2^(e+1). The top m bits of the mantissa determine one of the 2^m equal buckets within the octave.

According to recent reports, for example, here's the number 5.25 with m=3 (8 buckets per octave). In binary, 5.25 = 1.0101₂ × 2², so the exponent is 2 (stored as 1025), and the mantissa starts with 0101:.

It has been revealed that add finds the bucket for the given number and increases the count. Merge adds the counts bucket by bucket. Quantile adds up the counts from the closer end (the leftmost bucket for q ≤ 0.5, the rightmost bucket otherwise) until it reaches the rank.

Industry observers note that the number of mantissa bits m comes from the requested error: the constructor picks the smallest m for which the maximum error doesn't exceed the requested one. The default is m=7: 128 buckets per octave and an error of 0.39%.

A t-digest13 also estimates quantiles, but it limits the error in ranks: Quantile(0.99) returns a value whose rank is close to 99%. A log-linear histogram limits the error in values: Quantile(0.99) returns a value close to the true 99th percentile.

In a recent development, in the middle of the data, the two are pretty similar. But in a long tail, values at nearby ranks can be very different, so even a small error in rank can lead to a major difference in value. Here is the mean relative error of an 8.5 KB t-digest (δ=100) on 1M values from three distributions: lognormal (as in the benchmarks), Pareto with α=1.5 (a longer tail), and uniform between 1,000,000 and 2,000,000 (no tail):.

A log-linear histogram of about the same size (1% error, 8 KB) has an error below 0.78% for all these cases.

So a log-linear histogram is better for latencies, sizes, and other positive measurements with long tails. A t-digest is better when you need a fixed size no matter what the values are, or when the values can be arbitrarily close to zero.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks14, comparing unsure to hdr15 (log-linear, integers only, fixed range) and dd16 (DDSketch, logarithmic buckets) with a lognormal distribution (ns/op, lower is better):.

Mean relative error at the requested 0.1%, over 1M values (lower is better):.

Memory after adding 1M values (lower is better):.

Unsure adds values as fast as hdr and 5× faster than dd, queries 5–19× faster than hdr and about 35× faster than dd, and merges about as fast as dd and 35–175× faster than hdr. It's slightly less accurate than hdr (using 5× less memory), and more accurate than dd (using 1.4× more memory).

DDSketch paper by Charles Masson et al., 2019. ↩︎.

T-digest overview and how it works. ↩︎.

Log-linear histogram benchmarks. ↩︎.

In a recent development, hdrHistogram/hdrhistogram-go by Coda Hale. ↩︎.

It has been revealed that dataDog/sketches-go by Datadog. ↩︎.

MinHash estimates how similar two sets are. It summarizes each set in a short fixed-size signature (for example, 256 numbers). Comparing two signatures gives the approximate Jaccard similarity of the sets: |A∩B| / |A∪B|, the proportion of unique items that both sets share.

In a recent development, the size of a signature doesn't depend on the size of the set, so you can compare two sets of a million items each just by comparing 256 pairs of numbers instead of checking every item. Plus, each set's signature is only calculated once, so comparing lots of sets to each other is relatively cheap.

MinHash is useful for finding near-duplicate documents, like web pages or essays (represented as sets of words or 3-word phrases). It's also useful for finding similar user profiles (as sets of liked items) or overlapping datasets (as sets of keys).

Recent findings suggest that the MinHash sketch has one setting: the signature size k, which gives a standard error of √(J(1−J)/k) for true similarity J. For example, with k=256 and J=0.5:.

According to recent reports, you can add items to a sketch, merge sketches, and get and compare signatures. You cannot check if a specific item was added, count the items, remove them, or list them.

Classic MinHash17 hashes every item with k different hash functions. Here are two sets, A = {fox, cat, dog, owl} and B = {fox, dog, emu}, and their item hashes for k=4:.

Sources indicate that for each hash function, the set keeps only the smallest hash value among its items. These k minimums are the set's signature. To estimate the similarity of two sets, compare their signatures position by position, count the number of equal values, and divide by k:.

According to recent reports, the estimated similarity (0.5) is different from the actual value (2 shared items / 5 distinct items = 0.4). To get a more accurate estimate, k is usually much larger than in this example.

According to recent reports, one permutation hashing18 hashes every item once, with a single hash function, and splits the range of hash values into k equal buckets. Each bucket keeps the smallest hash value among its items. Here are the same sets with k=4, using h1 from above:.

Each bucket works like a separate MinHash over the items in its range. So the bucket minimums form a signature, and comparing two signatures works the same way. But there is a catch: when a set isn't much larger than k, some buckets end up empty (shown as · above), so there's nothing to compare in them.

Sources indicate that optimal densification19 solves this by filling each empty bucket with the value from another bucket in the same set. Each empty bucket tries other buckets in a pseudo-random order and copies the value of the first non-empty one:.

Industry observers note that this order depends only on the empty bucket's position, so two similar sets tend to fill empty spots with the same values. This makes the estimate work for sets of any size, with about the same error as classic MinHash.

It has been revealed that unsure keeps the k bucket minimums in the sketch. Add and Merge use the original buckets. Densification only happens in Signature, and it makes a copy of the buckets without modifying the sketch.

Each item is hashed once with 64-bit wyhash. Multiplying the hash by k once gives both the bucket and the value to store:.

Densification fills empty buckets in a coordinated way, spreading the copies evenly across the non-empty buckets. This keeps the error close to classic MinHash, and makes densification fast even for small sets.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks20, comparing unsure to dgryski21 (classic MinHash) (ns/op, lower is better):.

RMSE of the similarity estimate at k=256 and J=0.5 (lower is better):.

Unsure adds items 6–70× faster than dgryski, compares signatures at the same speed, has roughly the same accuracy, and uses half the memory.

According to recent reports, classic MinHash paper by Andrei Broder, 1997. ↩︎.

One permutation hashing by Ping Li et al., 2012. ↩︎.

Optimal densification paper by Anshumali Shrivastava, 2017. ↩︎.

Recent findings suggest that dgryski/go-minhash by Damian Gryski. ↩︎.

Bloom filter and HyperLogLog are everyone's favorites, but they're not the only useful probabilistic data structures out there. In some situations, you might find these helpful:.

To use them in Go, try the nalgeon/unsure package:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Recent findings suggest that local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this upcoming generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Recent findings suggest that support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too significant to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Industry observers note that reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

It has been revealed that API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

Industry observers note that while we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

In a recent development, the first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

Industry observers note that and if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Sources indicate that language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • It has been revealed that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

It has been revealed that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

According to recent reports, the catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch people had to work harder to get in.

Industry observers note that until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

Sources indicate that torchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

It has been revealed that the model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

Recent findings suggest that TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too substantial for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

Industry observers note that the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

According to recent reports, decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

Recent findings suggest that the Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an glitch on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 problems, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel aims. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch people. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

Recent findings suggest that we can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an problem and tell us about it.

Beyls: Wrapping up LLVM's relicensing effort

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lwn

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.
  • Sources indicate that we've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018.
  • Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

Sources indicate that we've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. Fresh contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...].

Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

In a recent development, the LLVM exception to Apache-2 Posted Nov 21, 2026 13:13 UTC (Sat) by coriordan (guest, #7544) [Link] For anyone who doesn't know (like me until 5 minutes ago): The LLVM exception: https://merlijn.sebrechts.be/blog/what-is-the-apache-2-ll... It indicates two things. (Based on my quick read; corrections welcome) 1. That Apache-2 licensed compilers (which insert some compiler code into the executables they create) don't create Apache-2 obligations for the programs they create. 2. It fixes incompatibility with GPLv2 by saying that, for a combined work of Apache-2 plus GPLv2 code, if an authority decides that any clause of Apache-2 is incompatible with GPLv2 then that clause of Apache-2 doesn't apply. (Which I guess they decided is fine because the places where there could be conflicts, such as patents, using the GPLv2 version isn't enough of a problem to be worth incompatibility.) So, the LLVM exception looks like a pretty good instrument.

#69532. Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1291 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

Industry observers note that the modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

It has been revealed that start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

It has been revealed that call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

Recent findings suggest that the table indicates which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Industry observers note that each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

According to recent reports, in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

Recent findings suggest that the system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

Sources indicate that in eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

Sources indicate that in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

Industry observers note that with @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

According to recent reports, the table demonstrates one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Industry observers note that both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In a recent development, in Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I love using JJ and recently I’ve found a cool way to handle TODOs that works for me.
  • Recent findings suggest that usually I’ll put them in a TODO.md file which is pretty standard.
  • In a recent development, JJ has a cool feature where you can make empty changes, and even write descriptions for them before actually doing work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I love using JJ and recently I’ve found a cool way to handle TODOs that works for me.

Recent findings suggest that usually I’ll put them in a TODO.md file which is pretty standard. But, I forget about this file swiftly and am not very good at remembering to cross stuff off. Also since it’s in-tree I’ll often not want to upgrade it, and then forget to do so later.

In a recent development, JJ has a cool feature where you can make empty changes, and even write descriptions for them before actually doing work. So what if I just make all the stuff I wanna do later as empty commits?

Pretty nice! When I want to start working on something I’ll rebase it out of my TODO tree and onto some other change.

I need to rebase my “TODO base” forward when i make changes, but because it’s empty it will never have conflicts and can pretty easily move around.

TODOs that depend on other TODOs also naturally fit here, I just make upcoming empty commits on top of other empty commits.

I have git.private-commits configured to make sure nothing with the private: prefix will get pushed. This ensures my TODOs stay on my local system. Of course, there are benefits to not doing this.

Anyway that’s about it, not very ground breaking but something I like.

#69529. How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2207 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2207 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • Recent findings suggest that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

Recent findings suggest that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

Sources indicate that one of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

In a recent development, the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

Sources indicate that the first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

It has been revealed that the second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping tech giant that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

According to recent reports, the third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

It has been revealed that and the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

It has been revealed that adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

It has been revealed that first, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

It has been revealed that second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping manufacturer: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

According to recent reports, an expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

It has been revealed that the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

It has been revealed that the lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

Sources indicate that vocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Sources indicate that specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News How Google Traced GKE API Timeouts to a Linux Kernel TCP Bug.

Nov 21, 2026 3 min read.

Google recently detailed how three interacting bugs across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, and the Linux kernel caused intermittent Kubernetes API connectivity failures, blocking around 800 developers from deploying to production.

In January, a customer running multiple GKE clusters with Private Service Connect (PSC) for private control-plane access experienced intermittent timeouts when pods attempted to reach the Kubernetes API server.

Industry observers note that packet captures revealed that the control plane was responding to fresh TCP connection requests with stale ACK packets belonging to previously closed connections. The root cause involved three separate bugs across different networking layers. Akash Thakur, senior technical solutions engineer at Google Cloud, describes how engineers across multiple Google teams identified three root causes and ultimately addressed them:.

It has been revealed that in a race to fix the problem, we involved engineers across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, networking, hostnet, kernel, and the Linux upstream community, who together tracked down not one but three distinct root causes. And the final fix landed not as a config change or a feature flag, but as a patch to the Linux kernel itself.

The investigation identified three interacting causes: packet reordering in PSC, Envoy's half-close behavior preventing TCP connections from being properly closed, and a Linux kernel bug that discarded certain reordered FIN packets.

It has been revealed that thakur describes a complex troubleshooting case involving I/O timeouts across Private Service Connect, virtual network interfaces, and the Linux TCP state machine, which ultimately revealed a kernel glitch leaving sockets stuck indefinitely in the FIN_WAIT_2 state. Thakur explains:.

Most networking cases resolve at one layer. You find the misconfigured firewall rule, the exhausted connection pool, the miscalculated MTU. You fix it and move on. This one was different because the symptom — i/o timeout on a connection that never completed — was the same whether you were looking at the Private Service Connect layer, the kernel's TCP state machine, or Envoy's connection management. Every layer had a plausible explanation, and every explanation was incomplete.

Sources indicate that the issue was addressed through three coordinated fixes over several weeks: Google first rolled back a Private Service Connect change to restore connectivity, then corrected the proxy protocol handling and added regression tests. Finally, a Linux kernel patch, authored by Eric Dumazet, formerly a software engineer at Google, fixed the underlying TCP issue. Rohan Karne, managing director at Google Cloud, comments:.

This is the unglamorous reality of mission-critical platform engineering—methodically ruling out the obvious suspects and digging into packet captures until you find the kernel root cause.

Sources indicate that thakur highlights how individually reasonable behaviors across networking, proxies and operating systems can combine into complex infrastructure failures. Packet captures at multiple network layers were essential to identifying the problem, while correlating network symptoms with infrastructure changes helped establish the connection between the three bugs. Guangba Yu, a postdoctoral researcher at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, highlights:.

Industry observers note that for AIOps and chaos engineering, the transferable method is organizing simultaneous path observations, protocol state, and rollout events while distinguishing symptom recovery from state-machine correction. This anonymized case supplies no population failure rate and does not explain all API timeouts.

Justin Garrison, field CTO at Sidero, notes:.

Industry observers note that at first I was excited to read this article that leads to a kernel patch which are always fun. It turns out GKE just runs a kernel from 3 years ago (6.1) and the bug was already fixed upstream and they had to backport it.

The kernel fix was merged into Linux 6.9.7 and backported to the 6.6 and 6.1 LTS branches, reaching GKE customers in version 1.33.5 and later.

Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3159 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Mentioned It Was Done.
  • We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
  • ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Mentioned It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

It has been revealed that figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Recent findings suggest that then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

In a recent development, so we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

It has been revealed that we call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

It has been revealed that table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

Sources indicate that what does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but organization policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

According to recent reports, thinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly latest solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 demonstrates which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

According to recent reports, table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

Sources indicate that the headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Sources indicate that average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

In a recent development, the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

In a recent development, overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

It has been revealed that table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

In a recent development, the move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

Industry observers note that the dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

It has been revealed that these results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Sources indicate that selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

In a recent development, every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Recent findings suggest that training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

It has been revealed that for the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

According to recent reports, zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

Recent findings suggest that that explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

In a recent development, why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

According to recent reports, A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

In a recent development, the question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

Recent findings suggest that so we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO enhancement.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

It has been revealed that when sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Recent findings suggest that nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In a recent development, in the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up
