General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Krebsonsecurity ↗ Open Full Page

Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned.
  • Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France.
  • In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

It has been revealed that the FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Sources indicate that rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

According to recent reports, multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

According to recent reports, on October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages demonstrated he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

Recent findings suggest that that source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats revealed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

Sources indicate that krebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. manufacturer or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology manufacturer that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

Industry observers note that the story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”.

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

In a recent development, according to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian manufacturer was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it highlights the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

Industry observers note that “If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT organization,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”.

In a recent development, an email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer mentioned the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”.

Recent findings suggest that the statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

Recent findings suggest that it is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Sources indicate that experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach indicates PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

Sources indicate that but that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool consumers, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the firm’s clients directly later on.

Industry observers note that the FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

According to recent reports, the following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”.

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately noted they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the manufacturer will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he noted, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

Recent findings suggest that “It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo remarked. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”.

Camillo remarked the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

It has been revealed that in recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to patch their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers.
  • The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress.
  • Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to patch their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare stated it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, stated “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security complications in recent memory.”.

Censys, a organization that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, noted a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz mentioned every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”.

It has been revealed that the Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz stated that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the firm worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

According to recent reports, “A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”.

Industry observers note that the SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology organization credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Revision, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1213 w)

Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1213 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google noted today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud.
  • A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) remarked Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
  • It has been revealed that the global distribution of XCPE botnet infections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google noted today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) remarked Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

It has been revealed that the global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

It has been revealed that the report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their owners with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”.

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google remarked it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm consumers, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

Sources indicate that another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy firm operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded tech giant in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

Recent findings suggest that the MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain fresh customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”.

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”.

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he remarked. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”.

Patch, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs remarked that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”.

The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any tech giant called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”.

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number.

#69433. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (777 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Krebsonsecurity ↗ Open Full Page

Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (777 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today.
  • Recent findings suggest that the security firm Layer3 Intel remarked it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650).
  • The proxy tracking company Synthient stated on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Recent findings suggest that the security firm Layer3 Intel remarked it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 revealed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient stated on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Recent findings suggest that synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

Industry observers note that there are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

In a recent development, layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel mentioned it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage indicated how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting customers.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”.

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end consumers, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox remarked it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

#69431. Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1984 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1984 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document.
  • According to recent reports, token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors.
  • Sources indicate that in this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up promptly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

According to recent reports, token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

Sources indicate that in this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

According to recent reports, pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

Industry observers note that A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

In a recent development, for example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:.

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d.

Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

Sources indicate that the useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

Recent findings suggest that hierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

In a recent development, these merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:.

In a recent development, with pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:.

This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

Sources indicate that adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Industry observers note that rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:.

Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

Sources indicate that pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:.

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​.

In a recent development, the first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives patch the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:.

In a recent development, cachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

Industry observers note that gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

In a recent development, multiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

Recent findings suggest that the poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

In a recent development, the complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:.

It has been revealed that the script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

In a recent development, this runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:.

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:.

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

Sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Recent findings suggest that let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:.

According to recent reports, the pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:.

Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

Recent findings suggest that I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

Sources indicate that at the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:.

Industry observers note that if the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

In a recent development, multiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

According to recent reports, with a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2211 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time.
  • Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment.
  • In a recent development, building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models.

Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4).

In a recent development, building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps users entirely in control of their digital lives.

Recent findings suggest that botPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

Learning from demonstrations (SFT).

Industry observers note that we first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

Industry observers note that next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages).

Sources indicate that finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

Industry observers note that the second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

In a recent development, each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

It has been revealed that botPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

Industry observers note that table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

In a recent development, tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

Sources indicate that table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

According to recent reports, botPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

It has been revealed that table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

In a recent development, the largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

Recent findings suggest that botPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

It has been revealed that botPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

It has been revealed that on complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

Sources indicate that complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

Recent findings suggest that botPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):.

Industry observers note that it does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

It has been revealed that botPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

Industry observers note that botPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

It has been revealed that [1] Yu, Qiying, et al. "DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025): 113222–113244.

Recent findings suggest that [2] Zhang, Shaokun, et al. "Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1: Exploring Tool-Using Language Models with Reinforced Reasoning." International Conference on Learning Representations (2026).

Sources indicate that [3] Qian, Cheng, et al. "ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025).

#69422. The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2541 w)
📖 Baca
