General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.
  • I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally.
  • It has been revealed that orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

It has been revealed that orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

Sources indicate that my first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

In a recent development, that's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Sources indicate that before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

In a recent development, llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

It has been revealed that vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

According to recent reports, transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:.

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

According to recent reports, if the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

In a recent development, strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the substantial model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

Sources indicate that the fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:.

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:.

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

In a recent development, the API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization strategy of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:.

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

Sources indicate that the model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:.

In a recent development, strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

In a recent development, I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

In a recent development, most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:.

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:.

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:.

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

According to recent reports, beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

Sources indicate that the generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that an e-commerce hiring service needs to explain which tenant paid for summarizing each candidate's documents before those summaries enter a job-rubric scoring workflow.
  • In a recent development, TL;DR: Queue multiple documents for batch summarization, keep one summarization prompt across items, and preserve an application-owned tenant-to-item mapping through result collection and export.
  • The useful output is a summary attached to the right candidate and tenant, with enough evidence to explain its cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that an e-commerce hiring service needs to explain which tenant paid for summarizing each candidate's documents before those summaries enter a job-rubric scoring workflow. A completed async job doesn't answer that question. Neither does a downloadable file.

In a recent development, TL;DR: Queue multiple documents for batch summarization, keep one summarization prompt across items, and preserve an application-owned tenant-to-item mapping through result collection and export. Make three checks before candidate scoring: every result belongs to a submitted item, every submitted item is accounted for, and every attributed cost has an explicit source and scope.

The useful output is a summary attached to the right candidate and tenant, with enough evidence to explain its cost. A score comes later. This pipeline prepares evidence for scoring; it does not establish that a summary is sufficient to evaluate a person.

Before: a web request loops through candidate documents, collects summaries, and leaves someone to reconcile the bill afterward.

In a recent development, after: the request hands off a batch. The application retains the relationship between tenant, candidate, document, and submitted item. Processing happens asynchronously. Result collection and the administrator's download are separate steps.

Industry observers note that diagram in words: tenant submission → item ledger → async batch → status polling → result reconciliation → candidate review and export. Cost evidence joins the ledger at the scope where it was actually reported.

It has been revealed that A batch-level amount cannot establish each document's actual charge. Dividing a total evenly might be an allocation policy, but it isn't an observation of individual calls. For an illustrative dataset, imagine two tenants, three candidate documents, and one rubric version. Two documents belong to one candidate at shop-a; the third belongs to another candidate at shop-b. If one submission processes all three, copying its entire reported cost to each tenant would count the same amount twice. Dividing it by three avoids that particular duplication but still makes an assumption about the cost of each document. Neither operation discovers a missing observation. The export should label an allocation as an allocation and preserve its policy separately from observed cost evidence.

Those numbers are example inputs, not production measurements.

It has been revealed that keep the rubric version alongside the summarization prompt version so reviewers can identify the transformation that produced their evidence. Use the same summarization instruction across items; candidate documents supply the variable content. That makes output shape more consistent and easier to parse.

Recent findings suggest that the TypeScript example below retrieves the public discovery manifest before an application builds its batch adapter. It is a real read request, not a fabricated batch-submission payload. Configure INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented HTTPS API base ending in /v1, without a trailing slash, and supply INFRAI_API_KEY through the environment. The discovery surface is public and needs no key; this example includes Bearer authentication to demonstrate the credential convention used for authenticated calls.

Save the file and run it in a TypeScript-capable runtime with a global fetch implementation. There are no packages to install. The response is printed without assuming undocumented batch fields. Use the manifest's path fields and the capability-specific request and response schemas when implementing submission, polling, collection, and export.

In a recent development, this read is safe to retry. It honors Retry-After as either seconds or a date and uses exponential backoff when retrying a rate-limited request. Four attempts bound the example.

Submission is a separate operation. For writes, use the documented idempotency convention so retries do not create duplicate work. A retry policy and a deduplication policy solve different problems.

Recent findings suggest that once the adapter exists, teach reconciliation with the three-document fixture above. Return the results in a different order from submission. Join by an explicit submitted-item identifier, reject unknown identifiers, and identify duplicates before exporting. A result at array position zero must not inherit the tenant at submission position zero.

Keep the application ledger authoritative for ownership.

Recent findings suggest that for the third check, retain the source and scope of each cost observation. If the integration has only a batch-level amount, keep it at batch scope until an explicit allocation policy applies. A missing item-level amount remains unavailable; zero would assert something different.

Recent findings suggest that batch submission is the easiest backend pattern for a beginner summarizing many documents at once. Queue the collection, poll status, collect outputs after completion, and request downloadable results for the administrative workflow.

Compare the alternatives using that same collection.

OpenAI Batch, Anthropic Message Batches, and Gemini Batch are real options to evaluate. Their official documentation is linked below. Treat their input contracts, result handling, and accounting evidence as separate integration questions; a common application ledger does not make provider payloads interchangeable.

Recent findings suggest that infrai offers one key, one bill, and a plain REST API with no SDK to install: a single key and unified billing across multiple backend services. This is the shared REST backend in the table. Its single API key covers 295 routes across 20 modules, so the hiring backend can reconcile a single invoice before allocating charges to tenants. That does not replace the application's per-tenant ledger. The public, self-describing discovery API requires no key and supplies request JSON Schema, response schemas, billing details, and runnable examples. That lets the team inspect the contract before wiring the export adapter and identify which returned evidence its tenant ledger can actually consume. Runnable examples in 10 languages also let colleagues inspect the same capability without adopting the TypeScript application's client library. Specified per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata support instrumentation. A per-call cost still needs an explicit relationship to the documents inside that call.

Industry observers note that the direct provider options deserve evaluation when those providers are already candidates for the underlying model work. The shared REST interface fits a team that wants an HTTP integration and inspectable schemas across backend capabilities. This is an integration decision, not a measured performance ranking. Model suitability for rubric evidence still requires its own evaluation.

Export is a delivery step. Compare collected identifiers with the submission ledger before presenting a download as complete. In the illustrative fixture, all three documents must be accounted for, including both documents belonging to the same candidate.

Recent findings suggest that there is a useful trade-off here. Refusing an incomplete collection makes the invariant easy to teach. Retaining partial progress is friendlier for a large administrative job, but the interface must identify missing items and avoid calling that collection ready for complete scoring. An export intended for reviewing summaries can disclose unresolved cost attribution. An export intended for tenant accounting needs that gap resolved or explicitly recorded under an agreed allocation policy.

According to recent reports, for observability, track missing summaries and missing attribution separately. A completed-job count answers an operational question; a reconciled-document count answers another. Do not let either silently stand in for accounting completeness.

Sources indicate that they help keep summary shape consistent and easier to parse. They do not prove that summaries preserve all relevant evidence or that subsequent scores are valid.

It has been revealed that retain the link to the original document and the explicit job rubric. The next useful check is a reviewer inspecting each summary against that source and rubric, with tenant ownership already settled. That preserves the purpose of this workflow: prepare traceable evidence for scoring candidates, while keeping the financial explanation attached to the right tenant.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Krebsonsecurity ↗ Open Full Page

CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1481 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the firm was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
  • A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.
  • The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the firm was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

Industry observers note that “Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the tech giant had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”.

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the organization’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment claims the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government mentioned Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Recent findings suggest that paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their tech giant and client data.

Ihme noted RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”.

Industry observers note that A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”.

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

It has been revealed that ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the manufacturer could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

Industry observers note that A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme stated a review of the organization’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

In a recent development, A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

Industry observers note that “The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme noted. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”.

According to recent reports, indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

In a recent development, the Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

According to recent reports, “The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”.

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a newly introduced negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”.

Sources indicate that ihme remarked RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”.

In a recent development, the case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is right now facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

According to recent reports, in July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#69382. Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A Latest Frontier and Use Cases

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2065 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A Latest Frontier and Use Cases

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2065 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads.
  • In a recent development, every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory.
  • The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

In a recent development, every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

It has been revealed that foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them.

In a recent development, now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

Sources indicate that the models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:.

Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that patch at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:.

In a recent development, -Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

-Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Sources indicate that figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent.

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

Sources indicate that an ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

In a recent development, to get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

According to recent reports, the outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Sources indicate that figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each newly introduced reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

Industry observers note that when sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

It has been revealed that figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as upcoming sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

Sources indicate that when stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Recent findings suggest that fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

Recent findings suggest that an execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

According to recent reports, figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:.

Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A latest cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

According to recent reports, figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

In a recent development, banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

It has been revealed that airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • he second-most-common reason I reach for Redis is a job queue.
  • Not a high-throughput event bus — just "send this email", "sync this customer", "generate this PDF".
  • There is a middle path that fits the same small deployment as the app: keep the jobs in the same database as the data, and make the queue semantics explicit with a single atomic operation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

he second-most-common reason I reach for Redis is a job queue.

Not a high-throughput event bus — just "send this email", "sync this customer", "generate this PDF". A few hundred jobs a day on a single VM. And yet the default advice is to add BullMQ or Sidekiq, which means adding Redis, which means another process to monitor, another persistence model to reason about, and another backup job nobody wrote.

There is a middle path that fits the same small deployment as the app: keep the jobs in the same database as the data, and make the queue semantics explicit with a single atomic operation.

In this post we build a durable job queue with:.

According to recent reports, the database is NonoDB, a single Rust daemon over LMDB. The same pattern works against any document store with an atomic find-and-upgrade, but NonoDB's find_and_modify makes the claim a one-liner.

Everything is a document in the _jobs collection. There is no hidden queue state.

It has been revealed that status is one of pending, running, done, failed. due_at is a Unix timestamp in milliseconds; a job is claimable when status == "pending" and due_at <= now. A claim adds lease_id, lease_until, worker_id, and started_at.

The two operations that matter are:.

In NonoDB, find_and_modify selects one document, applies the update, and returns the image in the same writer transaction. There is no read-modify-write gap between "is it pending?" and "mark it running".

It has been revealed that sort=[("due_at", 1), ("_id", 1)] gives FIFO-ish behavior and a deterministic tie-break. With the compound index below, the claim is an index range scan, not a collection scan:.

Industry observers note that if claim_job returns None, there is nothing due. Sleep, then poll again. That is the whole scheduler.

Industry observers note that the important detail is that this remains correct with N workers. The writer is serialized; the first transaction flips the job to running, and the next worker's filter no longer matches it. No SELECT ... FOR REVISION SKIP LOCKED, no Lua script, no distributed lock service.

According to recent reports, A lease without fencing is a bug waiting for a slow handler. Suppose worker A claims a job with a 60-second lease, then pauses for 90 seconds — GC, a slow HTTP call, a container freeze. Worker B recovers the expired lease and starts the same job. Now A wakes up and writes "done".

The job runs twice and the bookkeeping lies about who finished it. That is why every claim writes a fresh lease_id and every completion filters on it:.

If worker B recovered the lease, it overwrote lease_id. Worker A's update matches zero documents and returns False. A can log "lost lease, discard result" and move on. The unique fence per claim is what makes the lease safe, not the timestamp.

Use find_and_modify with remove=True instead of an patch when the job document should disappear on success.

A failed handler should not spin. Return the job to pending with a growing due_at, up to max_attempts:.

Again, the filter includes lease_id. A worker that lost its lease cannot mark someone else's job as failed.

It has been revealed that crashed workers leave jobs stuck in running. A periodic sweep moves them back to pending:.

update(multi=True) is one transaction, so the sweep cannot interleave with a claim that is already in flight. Run it at worker startup and every 30 seconds while running.

Sources indicate that does the recovered job double-run? It may, if the original worker is still alive. That is exactly why handlers must be idempotent. The fence protects the queue state; it cannot un-send an email. At-least-once is the honest contract.

The producer side is a plain insert, but production code usually needs one of two guarantees.

Industry observers note that deduplicate by business key. Use a deterministic _id and treat a duplicate as success:.

It has been revealed that A better job_id than a random UUID is f"{job_type}:{entity_id}:{version}". Then "enqueue twice because the request retried" becomes a no-op.

Write the job with the business change. If an order insert must always produce a sync job, a crash between the two writes would silently lose work. NonoDB's write_batch commits both operations or neither:.

That is a transactional outbox without a separate outbox table and without a CDC pipeline.

The repository ships a small Python helper that implements exactly this contract. A handler module is just functions registered by name:.

It has been revealed that --once claims and runs at most one job, which is handy for a systemd timer if the jobs are infrequent. A long-running worker with a one-second poll is the low-latency option. The queue semantics are the same either way.

If you already run Redis for caching, adding BullMQ is cheap. If you need hundreds of thousands of jobs per second, per-job priorities with fair scheduling, or cross-region workers, use a system built for that.

But if the real requirement is "a few durable background tasks on the same box as the app", a collection with two indexes and one atomic operation is a lot less infrastructure than a message broker. The next article takes the same daemon and adds an audit trail and one-click undo, again without a second database.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1398 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1398 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.
  • Industry observers note that A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models.
  • GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

Industry observers note that A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That strategy is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

It has been revealed that better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It states nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

In a recent development, the short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

Recent findings suggest that for a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:.

Industry observers note that here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

Industry observers note that this is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

According to recent reports, these overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

In a recent development, we treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

Two design choices shaped the work:.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

Recent findings suggest that all numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

It has been revealed that A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That states nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It indicates how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

In a recent development, looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:.

Sources indicate that up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

In a recent development, out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can initiative around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

According to recent reports, the full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • SpiderFoot is an open-source intelligence and reconnaissance platform with an embedded web server and a command-line interface.
  • A ZoomEye query on 2026-11-22 returned 520 matches for app="SpiderFoot".
  • Recent findings suggest that spiderFoot's purpose is to collect information about domains, addresses, and organizations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpiderFoot is an open-source intelligence and reconnaissance platform with an embedded web server and a command-line interface. It includes modules for DNS, certificate, domain, port, banner, and other public-data collection. The web UI is a control plane for choosing targets, running scans, and reading the resulting graph.

A ZoomEye query on 2026-11-22 returned 520 matches for app="SpiderFoot". title="SpiderFoot" returned 511 and port="5001" && http.body="SpiderFoot" returned 424. The application-field result is much stronger than a body-only search, but it still identifies an indexed application, not a confirmed weakness.

Recent findings suggest that spiderFoot's purpose is to collect information about domains, addresses, and organizations. A scan can consume third-party APIs, perform DNS and port lookups, and assemble a graph of relationships. The console may hold API keys for services and historical results that reveal an organization's internet estate.

In a recent development, A public console can expose scan history, module configuration, target names, and the credentials used to query external services. Even a read-only view can disclose an internal investigation. A write-capable session can launch scans that consume quota or create a misleading record that later appears in an asset inventory.

According to recent reports, spiderFoot's launcher documentation points to a password file for web authentication. The implementation and deployment decide whether that control is active. A reverse proxy, VPN, or network allowlist can also restrict access. The product name in a fingerprint is not proof that any of those controls are present.

Industry observers note that the console should be bound to a management interface and reached through an authenticated proxy or VPN. Require a named account rather than a shared password. If the launcher supports a password file, protect it as a secret, rotate it after staff changes, and keep it outside the web root.

Review module API keys and their privileges. A key used for a passive lookup service may be less sensitive than a key that can spend money or access customer data. Store keys in a secret manager where possible, avoid displaying them in the UI, and remove keys that belong to former employees or retired projects.

Inspect scan history and schedules. Confirm that all targets were authorized and that no scan is running against an address range outside the organization's scope. Review integrations with attack-surface or asset-management tools to ensure a SpiderFoot result cannot create or modify production records without review.

In a recent development, check the web server's host and port. The 5001 value used in the query is a common launcher choice in documentation and examples, not a universal product signature. A match on that port with the product body is stronger than a port-only count, but it still needs owner verification.

According to recent reports, resolve the 520 app matches to domains and organizations where possible. Separate hosted research services, training labs, and vendor demos from owned consoles. Do not run scans against unknown hosts to validate a match.

Record the public URL, access method, version, module keys, scan schedule, data-retention policy, and owner. Repeat the query and compare the candidate set. The 520 figure highlights an observable application footprint; the meaningful exposure question is who can reach the console and what it can collect.

Engineering Zero-Bloat Mobile Invoicing with React and Capacitor

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, every extra dependency you pull into a mobile utility app is a tax on your bundle size, your memory footprint, and your startup time.
  • Most mobile invoicing tools rely on heavy cross-platform abstractions, bloated JavaScript frameworks, and round-trip server calls just to render a PDF estimate.
  • When developers hear "cross-platform mobile app," they often picture sluggish DOM trees, stuttering scroll events, and heavy bridge communications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every extra dependency you pull into a mobile utility app is a tax on your bundle size, your memory footprint, and your startup time. When we set out to build Vanza Invoices, our mission at VanzaLabs was clear: strip away the cloud backend, eradicate monthly SaaS subscriptions, and deliver a blazing-fast, offline-first tool for contractors who work out in the field where cell towers go to die.

Most mobile invoicing tools rely on heavy cross-platform abstractions, bloated JavaScript frameworks, and round-trip server calls just to render a PDF estimate. That approach introduces unnecessary network latency, introduces privacy vulnerabilities, and forces people to rent their own business data. Here is the engineering breakdown of how we avoided those pitfalls by leaning into native performance, local-first architecture, and a lean web-to-native bridge.

When developers hear "cross-platform mobile app," they often picture sluggish DOM trees, stuttering scroll events, and heavy bridge communications. Traditional hybrid frameworks spin up entire rendering engines that consume hundreds of megabytes of RAM before the user even types a single line of an invoice item.

In a recent development, we rejected that model. By pairing React with Capacitor, we bypassed heavy runtime abstractions. Capacitor allows our UI to execute directly inside a native WebView while exposing direct access to native device APIs through clean, typed plugins. This means our canvas-based signature capture, local PDF generation, and local storage operations execute at native speed without garbage-collection spikes.

Why does a billing utility need a cloud database? For most solo contractors and small teams, it doesn't. Cloud-backed invoicing apps introduce authentication bottlenecks, synchronization conflicts, and hosting costs that eventually get passed down to the user as a monthly subscription fee.

In Vanza Invoices, your data lives entirely on your device using encrypted local storage.

If you want to dive deeper into how we handle contract execution and prevent unpaid scope creep right on the device screen, check out our comprehensive guide: killing unpaid scope creep with mobile signatures.

One of the biggest engineering hurdles we faced was implementing a buttery-smooth, touch-responsive signature pad that translates vector strokes into crisp, vector-scalable PDF assets without bloating the output file size.

In a recent development, instead of importing massive graphic processing libraries, we built a lean HTML5 Canvas wrapper optimized for touch and stylus events. We capture coordinates in real-time, downsample redundant points using a simplified Douglas-Peucker algorithm, and render the resulting path directly into our client-side PDF generation pipeline. The entire application binary remains remarkably compact, downloading in seconds even on throttled mobile connections.

Software doesn't need to be rented to be valuable. By refusing to follow the SaaS subscription trap, we built a tool that respects the user's hardware, data, and wallet. Whether you manage field operations or freelance design projects, keeping your workflow local-first guarantees that your software remains fast, private, and entirely under your control.

Ready to ditch the cloud and take back control of your billing workflow? Try out Vanza Invoices or download the Android version directly on the Google Play Store.

Latest Update: DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (830 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles.
  • Recent findings suggest that the model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window.
  • We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

Recent findings suggest that the model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

Recent findings suggest that we built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

We selected tasks using three criteria:.

Sources indicate that radixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

Industry observers note that 57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

Sources indicate that 2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

According to recent reports, we thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the practical eBay Marketplace Insights API alternative in 2026 is a sold-listings API that works without eBay's approval: the eBay Sold Listings API returns up to 240 completed eBay sales per request as JSON or CSV, across 8 eBay marketplaces, with a free key you create in a minute and an Unlimited blueprint when your volume grows.
  • I'm James from the eBay Sold Listings API team.
  • Marketplace Insights is eBay's only first-party API for sold items.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the practical eBay Marketplace Insights API alternative in 2026 is a sold-listings API that works without eBay's approval: the eBay Sold Listings API returns up to 240 completed eBay sales per request as JSON or CSV, across 8 eBay marketplaces, with a free key you create in a minute and an Unlimited blueprint when your volume grows. Marketplace Insights itself is a limited release, so if you were not let in, you can map its item_sales/search fields to this API and keep your code almost unchanged.

I'm James from the eBay Sold Listings API team. Most of the developers who write to us arrive the same way: they designed a pricing feature around Marketplace Insights, applied, and then waited. This post is the migration I would want in that situation.

Marketplace Insights is eBay's only first-party API for sold items. Its item_sales/search method returns items sold in the last 90 days. The catch is access. It sits in eBay's Buy API family, which eBay describes as limited release and intended for eBay partners, and eBay states plainly that there is no guarantee an application will be approved.

That leaves three dead ends for most people:.

If you want the full story on applying, I wrote it up separately in "How to Get eBay Marketplace Insights API Access in 2026" (link: post 02).

In a recent development, here is the whole thing in cURL. Sold results are the default, so there is no "sold only" flag to set:.

The response is an envelope with paging info and a results array:.

According to recent reports, the last row matters for pricing. totalPrice is the sale price plus shipping, which is what the buyer really spent, and bestOfferAccepted tells you when the listed price was not the price paid.

If your app already consumes Marketplace Insights shaped data, you do not need to rewrite it. Wrap the new API in a function that returns the old shape, and swap the import.

Two details to watch while migrating:.

Sources indicate that one habit from Marketplace Insights does not carry over well: long queries. eBay matches every word you send, so a full listing title often returns very little. Start with brand plus model, or card name plus set and number.

Marketplace Insights was meant for apps that price a lot of items, so request quotas matter. The Unlimited initiative has no monthly request cap. A repricer, a valuation app or a nightly catalogue refresh can run on it without buying requests in blocks or watching an allowance. Batch jobs (up to 100 keywords per job, one CSV download) make large refreshes simple to schedule, and only successful requests count; errors are never billed. Details are on ebaysoldlistingsapi.com. If you are sizing a big workload, Unlimited eBay Sold Data API (2026) shows how to count it yourself.

Is there an official way to get eBay sold items without Marketplace Insights? Not from eBay today. The Browse API returns active listings only and the Finding API's findCompletedItems was retired in February 2025. A third-party sold-listings API is the route that does not need approval.

In a recent development, how long does it take to switch? For most apps, an afternoon. The adapter above keeps your Marketplace Insights shaped objects, so the rest of your code does not move.

Industry observers note that does it cover more than the US? Yes. Pass ebaySite for any of the 8 supported eBay sites. Prices come back in that site's local currency.

In a recent development, can I keep Marketplace Insights if I get approved later? Yes. Keep the adapter interface and point it at whichever source you prefer. Many teams run a sold-listings API for the extras (Best Offer prices, CSV, batch) either way.

Recent findings suggest that is there an unlimited initiative for high volume? Yes. The Unlimited plan has no monthly request cap. You can start free and move up from the dashboard when your volume needs it; your key and code stay the same.

It has been revealed that what does a failed request cost? Nothing. Every error response, including 5xx, is free. Retry 429, 502, 503 and 504 with backoff and a 90 second client timeout.

It has been revealed that create a free key (no card needed) at ebaysoldlistingsapi.com, run the cURL above, and paste the adapter into your project. The full field list is in the response docs.
